catalog_locator: sec. 5.7 Tone, pp. 112, 117 (5.7.2 Functions of Tone in Chabu)
catalog_quote: As Chabu is a tonal language like its neighbouring Nilo-Saharan languages, in this chapter we present an overview of the tonology of the language. Chabu tone has never been treated. In the present study as well, we present a preliminary analysis of the basic features and roles of Chabu tone system. The detailed and exhaustive description of the Chabu tone system requires further study. Chabu has three level and one contour tones; High, Mid, Low and falling, which dominantly play a lexical function. ... Chabu seems to have only vowels as tone bearing units. Vowel length does not seem to have an effect on the tone melody of the lexeme. ... Monosyllabic words in Chabu are few in number. However, in monosyllabic nouns and verbs of Chabu all the three level (high, mid and low) tones are attested. ... The attested function of tone in Chabu is lexical and the following examples illustrate this…

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Chabu with an empty rule and no stress statements. This work adds that the language is tonal (lexical tone, one minimal pair há/hà) and is silent on word stress; it neither confirms nor contradicts any stress placement because none is recorded on either side.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The sketch's suprasegmental section covers only gemination (2.3.1), vowel length (2.3.2) and tone (2.3.3). It states that Shabo is a tonal language with lexical (not grammatical) tone, on the strength of one minimal pair; the words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the paper, and no statement is made about word-level prominence placement or about stress being absent. Some cited forms carry acute accents (dú 'breast', fù 'fall!', kotó 'girl', hà 'kill!'), which the author describes as tone marks (p. 374), not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The author notes the tone claim rests on a single lexical minimal pair and that grammatical tone was not found in his data; the data are described as scanty and tentative throughout (notes 1, 6 mention possible dialectal variation between informants Zelalem and Kernok, esp. in consonant and length).
new_statements.identity_note: The work calls the language Shabo (Bender's earlier name Mekeyir/Mikeyir; Majang exonym 'Mikeyir' = 'people who speak an unintelligible language'); data from informants Zelalem Taye, Kernok Imiru, Girmeye Kormi collected 1985-1990 near Gecha/Godare, Illubabor, Ethiopia. Note 6 records that informants differ (k vs h; single vs long segments), which the author says may indicate dialectal differences; he treats Kernok's data as more reliable. This is the same language as Glottolog shab1252 Chabu.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' rests on the only full grammar of Chabu (Kibebe 2015, 506-pp AAU dissertation, held as PDF+txt), and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated section and pages (5.7, p. 112; 5.7.2, p. 117). The dissertation contains no word-stress statement anywhere, and its own review of the earlier primary literature (Anbessa Teferra 1991, 1995) reports that those works also recognize lexical tone. No later or better phonological/prosodic study was found via Glottolog 5.1, Crossref (incl. the 2023 Oxford Handbook of Ethiopian Languages, which has no Shabo chapter), ERIC, or the Wikipedia bibliography; The unheld items (Teferra 1995, 9 pp; Teferra 1991, 17 pp; Aberra n.d. ms) are short, older, print-only or unpublished, and per Kibebe's summary agree on lexic
